chapter.title: Putting out the last fire: Japan, and why the Allies won

cards.body: Three days after the first atomic bomb, Japan's six top leaders were still split three against three: accept the Allied terms asking only to keep the emperor, or hold out for more conditions. On our street, Japan is the last house still burning. It shows the lesson of the whole war: **no single hose put the fire out**. Water had to hit it from every side at once.
cards.simpler: Three days after the first atomic bomb, Japan's six top leaders were still split. Three wanted to give up if Japan could keep its emperor. Three wanted to hold out for more. Picture the war as a street of burning houses. Japan is the last one still on fire. It shows the big lesson of the whole war: **no single hose put the fire out**. Water had to hit it from every side at the same time.

cards.prompt: It's 10 August 1945, and Japan has just offered to surrender, asking only to keep its emperor. Going by the street picture, what most likely tipped its leaders?

options.text: The first atomic bomb, on its own
Several blows landing in the same few days
Finally losing one big last battle

whyNot.a: That's one hose, not the whole street: after Hiroshima, Japan did not give in, and three days later its leaders were still split.
whyNot.c: That's what Japan's leaders were hoping for, not what happened: they wanted one bloody battle at home to win better terms.

cards.reteach: Picture the last burning house. One big hose soaks it and it keeps burning. It goes out only when water comes from every side, and Japan in August 1945 was like that: blockade, burned cities, bombs and a Soviet invasion, all at once.

cards.title: Doors nailed shut
cards.body:
From 1943 the Americans crossed the Pacific by *island-hopping*: they captured some islands for airfields and skipped others, leaving those garrisons to starve. Every step cost more. On Okinawa, from April to June 1945, about 12,000 Americans died, and far more Japanese soldiers and Okinawan civilians.

At the same time, American submarines and mines sank most of Japan's merchant ships, so oil and food stopped arriving. Bombers flying from the captured islands burned Japanese cities, which were built largely of wood.

By summer 1945 Japan was a house with **its doors nailed shut and the roof on fire**. Its leaders still hoped for one last battle.
cards.simpler: From 1943 America hopped across the Pacific, taking some islands for airfields and leaving others to starve. Each step cost more. On Okinawa, April to June 1945, about 12,000 Americans died, and far more Japanese and Okinawans. Submarines and mines sank most of Japan's cargo ships, cutting off oil and food. Bombers burned its mostly wooden cities. By summer Japan was a house with **its doors nailed shut and the roof on fire**. Its leaders hoped for one last battle.

cards.title: The week it ended
cards.body: On 6 August one American bomb destroyed Hiroshima, and Japan did not surrender. Just after midnight on 9 August, more than a million Soviet soldiers poured into Manchuria, Japan's puppet state in northeast China. That killed Japan's last hope, that Stalin would help arrange a peace. Late that morning a second bomb hit Nagasaki. That day the six leaders split three against three: accept the Allied terms asking only to keep the emperor, or demand four conditions. That night **the emperor, Hirohito, broke the tie** for the single condition, and on 14 August he settled it for good. On 15 August his voice came over the radio, the first time most Japanese had ever heard it, saying with world-class understatement that the war had not necessarily gone Japan's way. Historians still argue whether the bombs or the Soviet attack mattered more, and many conclude it took both. The surrender was signed on 2 September aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay.
cards.simpler: On 6 August an American bomb destroyed Hiroshima, and Japan fought on. Just after midnight on 9 August, over a million Soviet soldiers stormed Manchuria, Japan-run land in northeast China. That ended Japan's hope that Stalin would help make peace. Then a second bomb hit Nagasaki. The six leaders split three against three: give up if Japan could keep its emperor, or hold out for more. That night **the emperor, Hirohito, broke the tie** for giving up, and on 14 August he made it final. On 15 August most Japanese heard his voice for the first time, on the radio. Historians argue whether the bombs or the Soviets mattered more; many say both. The surrender was signed on 2 September aboard the USS Missouri.

cards.prompt: At dinner, a friend says: Japan surrendered because of Nagasaki, full stop. Which reply uses this chapter's idea best?

options.text: Right, the second bomb was the one that counted.
Nagasaki hit the same day as a Soviet invasion, on top of a blockade and burned cities. It was the pile-up.
No, it was only the Soviet invasion. The bombs didn't matter.

whyNot.a: That's the loudest hose, not the whole street: the Soviet invasion began that very same day.
whyNot.c: That's swapping one single cause for another: the bombs mattered too, and historians still argue about how much.

cards.reteach: Ask what landed in the same week, not which blow was loudest. Nagasaki, the Soviet invasion, the blockade and the burned cities all hit together. A good answer names the pile-up.

cards.title: Four hoses
cards.body:
You'd think the most powerful weapon ever made would end a war by itself. It didn't, in Japan or anywhere else.

Zoom out and the whole war ended the same way. Richard Overy argues the Allies didn't win just by having more; they learned to use it better. **Four hoses:** an alliance of Britain, the Soviet Union and America that Germany couldn't match. The Soviet army, which fought most of Germany's army: picture thousands of Soviet tanks meeting the Germans at Kursk in 1943. Factories that out-built the Axis: one American cargo ship, a Liberty ship, was put together in under five days. And control of the sea and air: the submarines and bombers that nailed Japan's doors shut.
cards.simpler: The most powerful weapon ever made didn't end the war alone. Zoom out and the whole war ended the same way. Richard Overy argues the Allies won by using their strength better, not just by having more. **Four hoses:** an alliance of Britain, the Soviet Union and America; the Soviet army fighting most of Germany's, like the thousands of Soviet tanks at Kursk in 1943; factories that out-built the enemy, where one American cargo ship was built in under five days; and control of sea and air, the submarines and bombers that cut Japan off.

cards.body: Someone at a pub quiz writes the atomic bomb as the answer to what ended the Second World War, and moves on. They picked the loudest hose and forgot the rest of the street: in Europe the bomb played no part, because **Germany had surrendered three months before Hiroshima**. How to spot it: if one answer explains a six-year war across two oceans, something is missing.
cards.simpler: Someone at a pub quiz writes "the atomic bomb" as what ended the Second World War, and moves on. They picked the loudest hose and forgot the rest of the street. In Europe the bomb played no part, because **Germany had surrendered three months before Hiroshima**. Here is how to spot this mistake: if one answer explains a six-year war across two oceans, something is missing.

cards.prompt: A friend asks why the Allies won, and you get one sentence. Which is best?

options.text: Because America built the atomic bomb.
Several pressures at once: an alliance, the Soviet army, factories, and control of the sea and air.
Because German and Japanese soldiers ran out of courage.

whyNot.a: That's the last hose, not all of them: Germany surrendered three months before Hiroshima.
whyNot.c: That's morale, not the hoses: even in summer 1945, with its doors nailed shut, Japan's leaders still hoped for one last battle. Courage was never what ran out.

cards.reteach: The war was too big for one cause. Germany surrendered before an atomic bomb was ever used, and Japan needed several blows at once. The Allies won by combining an alliance, the Soviet army, factories, and the sea and air.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Japan gave up in August 1945 because **the blows landed together**: a blockade, burned cities, two atomic bombs and a Soviet invasion in the same week. The Allies won the whole war the same way, with an alliance, the Soviet army, factories and control of the sea and air, every hose at once.

Next: open a single-volume history, like Beevor's, and see if your map holds.
cards.simpler: Japan gave up in August 1945 because **the blows landed together**: a blockade cutting off supplies, burned cities, two atomic bombs and a Soviet invasion, all in the same week. The Allies won the whole war the same way, with an alliance, the Soviet army, factories and control of sea and air, every hose at once. Next, open a one-book history of the war, like Beevor's, and see if your map holds up.

cards.body: Tonight, set a 10-minute timer and tell the whole war out loud, to a friend or your phone's voice recorder, from 1919 to 2 September 1945. Count your turning points. Aim for eight.
cards.simpler: Tonight, set a timer for 10 minutes and **tell the story of the whole war out loud**, to a friend or into your phone's voice recorder. Start in 1919 and finish on 2 September 1945. Count the turning points you mention, the moments where things changed direction. Aim for eight.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain how the Pacific war ended and give four reasons the Allies won, each tied to a chapter you have read.

dubious_claims: Card 1 and card 5 say the six leaders split three against three on 'whether to surrender'. In fact all six were ready to accept the Allied surrender terms in some form. They split over whether to ask for one condition (keeping the emperor) or four.
Exercise 1 says Japan's leaders 'agreed to give up' on 10 August. On that day Japan only sent a reply that still asked to keep the emperor. The final decision came on 14 August.
Exercise 1 feedback says 'after Hiroshima, Japan's leaders kept arguing for three more days'. The six leaders did not formally meet until 9 August.
Card 3 says island-hopping started 'from 1942'. The strategy of skipping islands mostly began in 1943; 1942 was Guadalcanal.
Exercise 3 feedback says Japanese soldiers on Okinawa fought 'almost to the last man'. Over 7,000 surrendered, and the chapter never teaches this fact.
repairedFrom.why: Card 6, 'Four hoses', tries to do two jobs: it finishes the argument about Japan's surrender, then lists four abstract causes with chapter numbers in brackets, and offers nothing to picture.
repairedFrom.fix: Move the bomb-versus-Soviet-invasion argument into card 5. Drop the chapter numbers and give each hose one concrete picture, for example a Liberty cargo ship built in under five days for factories, or Soviet tanks at Kursk for the Soviet army.
